## Design

### 2026-10-15 – During this 2-hour session, I focused on learning how 3D printers work and how their mechanics affect part design for the Mechanical Iris Container V1.

**2h**

During this 2-hour session, I focused on learning how 3D printers work and how their mechanics affect part design for the Mechanical Iris Container V1.

Here is what I worked on:

Understanding 3D Printing Mechanics: Researched key concepts like layer heights, wall thickness, bridging, and how print orientation impacts part strength.

Designing for 3D Printing (DfAM): Studied how horizontal and vertical tolerances work, specifically learning why clearance gaps (around 0.2 mm) are essential for moving parts not to fuse together.

Mechanism Planning: Evaluated how to orientationally break down the mechanical iris blades and body so they print cleanly without needing excessive support structures.

Next Steps: Start modeling the base container and test pin tolerances with small sample prints.

### 2026-10-15 – 8-Hour Intensive CAD & Prototyping Session

**8h**

8-Hour Intensive CAD & Prototyping Session

Today I did a deep-dive, 8-hour marathon session to fully design and prep the Mechanical Iris Container V1 from scratch.

1. Research & Kinematics (2

![Capture d’écran 2026-10-15 223611](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/93SZ6629c79TTcSGjVsViUEFCp6VxRI9/5ae8c0846d672fd2609af8061bbab4c9dbadf96b3569910830dd14bb0e26f260.png)

.5h):

Studied mechanical iris linkages, pin-in-slot motion, and guide track curves.

Calculated required clearance tolerances (~0.2 mm) to prevent moving parts from fusing on FDM printers.

2. Full CAD Modeling in 3D (3h):

Modeled the main outer cylinder and inner guide tracks with precise constrained sketches.

Designed the driving ring, the individual overlapping iris blades, and integrated rotation pins.

Assembled all parts digitally in CAD and ran a motion simulation/interference check to ensure the blades open and close smoothly without hitting each other.

3. Slicer Optimization & Print Preparation (1.5h):

Imported all components into the slicer (Bambu Studio).

Configured print settings: fine layer height (0.16 mm) for smooth sliding tracks, optimized wall count, and adjusted seams to avoid mechanical friction.

Set up variable layer heights and tested print-in-place vs. multi-part layout strategies to minimize support material.

4. Design Revisions & Troubleshooting (1h):

Discovered a clearance issue with blade overlap during assembly check.

Adjusted the blade chamfers and pin tolerances in CAD, then re-sliced the whole assembly.

Next Steps: Launch the full print job and assemble the mechanical iris!
